## Overview

In this graded assignment, you will practice with shell scripts, shell variables,
containers, modules, and version control.

## Directions and grading

### Submission expectations

- **Deadline**: [Sunday Oct 11^th^ at 11:59 pm]{style="background-color: #faf678;"}.
- **Submission**: You will submit your assignment by tagging the instructor in an
  Issue in your GitHub as per the last step below.

## Detailed steps

### General

Just like for the previous graded assignment:

- Execute Unix shell and Git commands to answer all questions unless explicitly
  instructed otherwise.

- When you issue a command in the terminal, include the command
  in a Markdown code block, and the command's output in another code block.
  However, this isn't needed for some Git commands.
  To avoid confusion and make life easier for you,
  we provide you with a **template Markdown file** where you can add your answers
  (see question 1), which contains code blocks wherever needed.

  ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
  ### A worked example of how to answer a question when you ran a command _(Click to expand)_

  **Assignment questions:**

  1. Print your current working directory to screen.

  **Your answers as part of your Markdown document:**

  ````bash-in-nocolor
  ### 1: Print your current working directory to screen

  ```bash
  pwd
  ```

  The output of the command was:

  ```
  /fs/ess/PAS3493/people/jelmer
  ```
  ````
  <hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
  :::

- Keep a **Markdown preview** open to the side while you work,
  so you can check that your answers render as you intended ---
  especially the code blocks.

### Setting up

- Start a VS Code (Code Server) session at OSC OnDemand as per usual,
  and open a terminal in that session.

- Create a new dir for this assignment, `/fs/ess/PAS3493/people/$USER/GA3`,
  and navigate there. **This will be your working dir for the entire assignment.**

### Part A: Your README, data, and Git repo

01. Copy the **template file** for this assignment,
    `/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/GA3/GA3_template.md`, into your working dir as
    `README.md`.
    Open it in the VS Code editor and modify its title
    (the level 1 header inside the file) to include **your name**.

    _You'll use this file throughout the assignment to add your answers_
    _(remove the instructional comments inside the file as you go:_
    _these are Markdown comments, i.e. text between `<!--` and `-->`,_
    _which is hidden in the Markdown preview)._

03. Inside dir `GA3`, also create dirs `data`, `scripts` and `results`.
    Next, let's copy some data files to make your dir self-contained,
    like a typical situation for a research project:

    ```bash
    cp -v ../garrigos/fastq/S63* data/
    cp -v ../garrigos/meta/metadata.tsv data/
    ```

04. Initialize a Git repository.
    Commit to the repo throughout the assignment as you see fit,
    but at least once for each "Part" of this assignment.
    Use and commit a `.gitignore` file as you see fit.

### Part B: Running two scripts

05. Save the script below as `scripts/echo.sh`.
    Look at the below three commands to run the script,
    and describe what you expect to be the output and why.
    Then, test the commands and if any output was not as expected,
    reconcile the differences.

    - The script:

      ```bash
      #!/bin/bash
      set -euo pipefail

      echo "$1"
      echo "$2"
      echo "$3"
      echo "Finished"
      ```

    - The commands:

      ```bash
      bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08
      bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 Oct09 Oct10
      bash scripts/echo.sh Oct07 Oct08 "Oct09 Oct10"
      ```

07. Write a shell script `scripts/printline.sh` that accepts two arguments,
    a file path and a line number,
    in order to _print_ (not store in a file) the requested line from the specified file.
    Don't make the script print anything other than the requested line from the file,
    and make sure to include the discussed best-practice header lines.

    _Hint: Figure out a way to combine `head` and `tail` to print one specific line from a file._
    _If you don't manage to, your script can instead print all lines up until the specified line,_
    _so you can still move on to the next two steps._

08. Test your `printline.sh` script twice by making it print two different lines
    from the `data/metadata.tsv` file you copied above.
    In one of these tests,
    redirect the script's output to an appropriately named file in `results`.

### Part D: Containers

The program "TrimGalore", which you'll use in the next few weeks of the course,
trims and filters FASTQ files to remove adapters,
poor quality bases, and short reads.
Here, you'll find and test-run containers with two different versions of this program.

10. Go to <https://seqera.io/containers> and find a container image for the program
    (default, i.e. latest, version).
    Back in VS Code, test-run the container with the command `trim_galore -v`.

11. It turns out that your collaborator has been using an older version of TrimGalore
    to trim other FASTQ files in the same project,
    so you decide that it will be best if you use that same version as well.
    Find a container for TrimGalore version 0.5.0 and test-run it with the
    same command as above.
    Are the versions printed in both cases as expected?

### Part E: Summarizing FastQC results with MultiQC

MultiQC is a very useful program that summarizes per-sample results of FastQC
and other bioinformatics programs into a single report where you can easily compare
samples.

12. Is MultiQC available as an OSC **module**?
    Check with `module spider`, and then also search for it in the
    OnDemand Module Browser, which covers all OSC clusters.

13. Using the FastQC module, run FastQC on **the two FASTQ files you copied** into `data`
    (not on the concatenated file from question 6)
    with a single command, writing the output to `results/fastqc`.

    <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for a hint._</summary>

    FastQC accepts multiple FASTQ files as arguments,
    the same way a command like `touch` does,
    so you can either type out the two filenames or use a glob pattern.

    </details>

14. Get a Seqera **container** with the most recent version of MultiQC,
    and use it to run `multiqc --version`.

15. MultiQC takes a **directory with results** from programs like FastQC as an argument.
    Get MultiQC's help info by running `multiqc --help` with your container.
    Use this information to figure out how to run MultiQC on your `results/fastqc` dir,
    with its output files in `results/multiqc`.

16. Run your MultiQC command. It will print some logging information to the screen ---
    how many FastQC reports does it report finding, and does that match what you expected?

17. List MultiQC's output files, then **open the HTML report** in VS Code
    (right-click > "Open Preview").
    How does it compare to the individual FastQC reports?
    <!-- TODO: check that the MultiQC report looks OK in the HTML Preview extension -->

18. Get a single Seqera container that contains **both** FastQC and MultiQC,
    and check that you can run both programs with it.
    Compare this container's URI with the URIs of the single-program containers you used above.
    What information is missing from it, and how could you still find that information?

### Part F: Modules and Pandoc

You'll practice with OSC software modules and the program Pandoc,
which can render Markdown files to HTML and PDF.

19. See if Pandoc is available at OSC prior to loading anything,
    and if so, which version, by running `pandoc -v`.
    Then, search the internet to check if that Pandoc version is the most recent one.

20. Check what other versions of Pandoc are available in OSC Lmod modules,
    and load the module with the most recent available Pandoc version.

21. Use the below Pandoc command to create a PDF of your `README.md`,
    and check whether the PDF file is there.

    ```bash
    pandoc -o README.pdf README.md
    ```

22. To view PDF files in VS Code, you'll first need to install a VS Code extension.
    Install the extension "_Papyrus PDF Preview_", and take a look at your PDF.
    Then, download the PDF file to your computer and also take a look at it there.

23. Does everything in the rendered PDF look OK?
    Or did you make formatting errors, or did anything else not render as expected?
    If so, update your Markdown file, rerender the PDF, and check again.

### Part G: Publish your repo on Github

You'll publish your Git repo on GitHub and "hand in" your assignment by creating
an Issue.

24. Create a repository on GitHub, connect it to your local repo,
    and push your local repo to GitHub.

25. Create a new issue and tag GitHub users `kstarr791` and `jelmerp`,
    asking Kelsey and Jelmer to take a look at your assignment.
